mainEntity.name: What is a cryptographic hash function?

acceptedAnswer.text: A cryptographic hash function maps an input of any size to a fixed-length digest. It is deterministic, one-way (pre-image resistant), and collision resistant — making it infeasible to reverse the output or find two inputs that produce the same hash.

SHA-1 is cryptographically broken for collision resistance. Google's 2017 SHAttered attack demonstrated a practical SHA-1 collision. It should not be used for digital signatures or certificate fingerprints, but remains acceptable for non-security-critical checksums.

mainEntity.name: Which SHA-2 variant should I use?

acceptedAnswer.text: SHA-256 is the right default for most applications. Use SHA-384 or SHA-512 when a compliance requirement mandates a larger digest. SHA-224 is a truncated form of SHA-256 for constrained environments.

mainEntity.name: Are SHA hashes safe for passwords?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. SHA functions are designed to be fast, which makes them unsuitable for password storage. Use a slow, purpose-built algorithm such as bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 instead.

mainEntity.name: How does SHA2Kit protect my data?

acceptedAnswer.text: All hashing runs entirely inside your browser using hash-wasm, a WebAssembly library. No text, file content, or hash output is ever transmitted to any server.
